prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: 华东区门店2024年1—5月销量 (language zh-CN).
Grid: 6 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 17px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "门店" · longest unbreakable word 18px · one-line width 105px
  col 2: header "1月" · longest unbreakable word 39px · one-line width 39px
  col 3: header "2月" · longest unbreakable word 38px · one-line width 38px
  col 4: header "3月" · longest unbreakable word 38px · one-line width 38px
  col 5: header "4月" · longest unbreakable word 39px · one-line width 39px
  col 6: header "5月" · longest unbreakable word 39px · one-line width 39px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 392px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 391px.
Fixed: content, font, 17px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"good","why":"Two-line rows stay compact and the month columns comfortably hold every four-digit value, but the 3+2 wrap cuts through store/branch names (上海徐/汇店, 杭州西/湖店), which slows row identification."},"B":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"The narrow first column preserves natural two-character chunks, but most store names need three lines, making rows tall and the table slower to scan while the month columns carry unused width."},"C":{"grade":"good","why":"The wider first column keeps four-character place/branch names intact and all numbers still fit; the main flaw is the isolated 店 suffix on several second lines, which is awkward but readable."},"D":{"grade":"good","why":"Same as C: strong preservation of 上海徐汇, 杭州西湖, 苏州观前, etc., with all numeric columns fitting; the lone 店 on the second line is the visible typographic compromise."},"E":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Like B, it breaks labels into natural two-character chunks but forces three-line rows and leaves the numeric columns wider than necessary, so the table reads tall and the first column feels cramped."}},"best":["C","D"],"confidence":"medium","unsure":"C and D look identical at this resolution; I may be missing a few pixels of difference. The main judgment call is whether C/D's intact four-character names outweigh the orphaned 店 suffix compared with A's more balanced but semantically disruptive 3+2 breaks."}
